The risks cannot be eliminated entirely, but they can be substantially reduced. In the context of a warming climate and rapidly changing mountain environment, that should be the priority.
(With inputs from Kunal Shankar)

title: Harvesting the Future: Mechanisation, Free Trade, and Policy Changes in Agriculture

content.value: Despite achieving record foodgrain production, India’s agriculture sector remains caught in a paradox of persistent farmer poverty and escalating vulnerability. The e-book, Harvesting the Future: Mechanisation, Free Trade, and Policy Changes in Agriculture, provides a multi-faceted analysis of its critical state. Authored by policy experts, scientists, and leaders, the essays in this e-book touch upon a wide range of topics — from climate change impact and the food security debate to farmer distress and the adoption of modern technology.

The book also takes a critical look at past and present government policies, from the Green Revolution’s legacy to recent initiatives like PM-KISAN and other controversial farm laws. But moving beyond a mere diagnosis of agrarian distress, the book also proposes a new, integrated vision for agriculture. It argues that addressing structural threats requires a fundamental “system” transformation rather than siloed, production-centric initiatives. It calls for a holistic “food systems” approach that balances economic viability, ecological sustainability, and nutritional security.

By exploring the intersections of technology infusion, cooperative movements, and robust, equitable policy frameworks, it provides a comprehensive roadmap for a more resilient, sustainable, and democratic agricultural future that places the farmer’s livelihood firmly at its centre.
What’s inside?
• Fields of uncertainty: India’s agriculture waiting for a ‘system’ transformation by T. Nandakumar
• Promoting Aquaculture technology infusion and start-ups in India by Abhilaksh Likhi
• India needs a new architecture to manage increasing compound climatic risks in agriculture by Pramod Kumar Aggarwal
• Digital technologies and automation in Indian farming: current status and adoption by Devinder Dhingra
• Between food security and free trade: Indian agriculture at the WTO and beyond by Poornima Varma
• The agrarian question in neoliberal India: farmers’ resistance and the struggle for democratic transformation by Ashok Dhawale
• Punjab’s new farm policy: agricultural development through cooperatives by Sukhpal Singh

title: Farmers block NH-16 in Ongole seeking remunerative prices for tobacco

content.value: Demanding remunerative prices for Virginia tobacco, hundreds of farmers blocked national highway (NH) 16 at Tangutur toll plaza near Throvagunta in Ongole on Wednesday. Consequently, several vehicles were stranded for kilometres along the highway.

Speaking to the media during the protest, Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM) Prakasam district committee convener Chunduri Ranga Rao alleged that Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu had failed to show even a minimal response, despite tobacco farmers staging various forms of protests.

“The SKM has organised several protests over the past three months demanding the State government to offer remunerative prices for tobacco. The Chief Minister recently announced that low-grade tobacco will be procured at ₹110 per kg, while its average price stands at ₹1,877 per kg,” he said.

The farmer leader demanded the Chief Minister to explain the underlying reason for the sudden reduction of the low-grade tobacco price to ₹110 per kg. He sharply criticised Mr. Naidu for feigning concern for farmers while making decisions that benefit corporate traders.

Mr. Ranga Rao pointed out that although the Mr. Naidu had previously issued orders mandating an average purchase price of at least ₹200 per kg for tobacco, not a single tobacco trader had actually complied with his directives.

He criticised corporate businessmen for dictating terms to the Central and State governments, noting that the governments themselves were subservient to these corporate interests. He demanded the both the governments to allocate ₹1,000-crore fund, and facilitate the tobacco procurement.

Speaking on the occasion, CPI Prakasam district secretary R. Venkat Rao said that the tobacco farmers in the State had paid thousands of crores of rupees to the Central and State governments in the form of penalties. “The tobacco exports generate lakhs of crores in foreign exchange for the country. The Central government, which waives loans worth lakhs of crores of rupees for corporate entities, could not allocate a mere ₹1,000 crore for tobacco farmers,” he questioned.

title: Kerala creates 11-member, Chief Secretary-led State AgriStack Data Governance Committee for farm sector

content.value: The Kerala government has created a 11-member State AgriStack Data Governance Committee (SADGC) headed by the Chief Secretary which will act as the institutional architecture for handling crucial data associated with the State’s agriculture sector.

The panel’s constitution is in line with a set of operational guidelines issued by the Union government to State and Union Territories in September 2025 to assume full ownership of the AgriStack operational backbone under the ‘State Core Handover Support’ programme. In the initial phase, the Centre wanted States to discharge “fiduciary, approval and oversight functions” through a committee-based or departmentally anchored mechanism, such as the SADGC.

The Chief Secretary-led panel will function as the empowered body to exercise these functions in Kerala, the Agriculture Department said in a July 25 order. It will act as the “fiduciary custodian of all AgriStack data within the State, held in public trust for farmers and farming communities.”

The Union government had conceived AgriStack, which is a digital public infrastructure (DPI), as “a single source of truth for farmer identity, land and their crops.” It was envisioned by the Centre as one of the two pillars of its Digital Agriculture Mission. AgriStack contains three foundational registries or databases connected with the agriculture sector; a farmers’ registry, geo-referenced village maps, and crop-sown registry. The relevance of an institutional mechanism such as SADGC lies in the fact that the AgriStack data would be leveraged by the government for implementation of agricultural schemes and disbursement of subsidies.

The Additional Chief Secretary and Agricultural Production Commissioner will act as the member secretary of the panel. It has as its members secretaries of the Revenue, Law and Electronics and Information Technology departments, the directors of Agriculture, Kerala State IT Mission, Survey and Land Records, and the Kerala State Remote Sensing and Environment Centre, the Land Revenue Commissioner and the State coordinator of the National Informatics Centre.

Other duties of the committee include approving or rejecting requests for AgriStack data access and use, prescribing State-specific conditions, safeguards and compliance requirements for data use, and serving as the nodal authority for coordination with the Centre.

title: India’s policy on urea | Explained

content.value: Amid concerns of fertiliser shortage during the ongoing kharif season due to the situation in West Asia, greater demand because of El Niño and complaints of over-use of chemical fertilisers such as urea, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs recently approved the National Investment Policy for Urea (NIPU)-2026.

The new policy is aimed at self reliance in urea production, a sector which is dependent on imports. According to the Government, the policy will encourage new investments in the urea sector for setting up the gas based urea manufacturing units in the country.

The key changes in the policy, compared to the existing policy, include the separation of fixed and variable costs for greater transparency, introduction of a viable Return on Equity (RoE) band with a floor at 12% and a ceiling at 16%, and mitigation of foreign exchange risk through conversion of fixed cost into Indian Rupees after four years based on prevailing exchange rates.
India’s urea policy
The Union Government had announced announced such a policy for urea sector in 2012, 2013 and it was amended in October 2014 to facilitate fresh investment.

Six new urea units have been set up under the 2012 policy, which includes four set up through Joint Venture Companies (JVC) of nominated PSUs and two set up by the private companies. At present, there are 33 operational urea manufacturing units with total reassessed/installed capacity of 269.42 Lakh Metric Tonnes (LMT), according to the Union Fertilisers Ministry.

“There is a need to increase the indigenous production of Urea. There is a gap in the indigenous production and demand of urea in the country which is filled by the import of urea,” the Government had said. It adds that total indigenous urea production capacity (Reassessed Capacity, RAC) has increased from 207.54 LMT per annum during 2014-15 to 269.42 LMT per annum during 2026-27.

The Government amended the policy further May 2015 for the existing 25 gas-based urea units and it led to additional production of urea by 20-25 LMT as compared to the production during 2014-15 annually.

From 225 LMT per annum during 2014-15, the current production from all these units has reached 314.07 LMT during 2023-24. “During 2025-26, 293.30 LMT of Urea was produced in the country,” the Government says.
Fertiliser subsidy

The total fertilisers subsidy in 2025-26 is ₹ 2,17,281.10 crore. In 2024-25, it was ₹ 1,77,162.06 crore. Out of this, the urea subsidy alone for 2025-26 was ₹ 1,42,175.74 crore and for 2024-25 it was ₹ 1,24,319.50 crore. For Phosphorus, and Potassium, the subsidy component is ₹ 74,999.99 crore and ₹ 52,810 crore respectively. For promotion of organic fertilisers, the Government provided a subsidy of ₹ 105.37 crore and ₹ 32.56 in the last two financial years.
Availability of Urea

According to the data provided by the Government in Parliament, as on March 3, 2026, the country has the requirement of 370.84 LMT of urea for the kharif season. The availability is 432.44 LMT, out of which 381.59 LMT will be for sale under Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system where all subsidised fertilisers will be sold to buyers is made through Point of Sale (PoS) devices “installed at each retailer shop and the beneficiaries are identified through Aadhaar Card, KCC, Voter Identity Card etc”. In 2024-25, the requirement was 364.01 LMT and availability was 443.83 LMT.

The Government claims it has taken steps to promote balanced and efficient use of fertilisers. “The Government is promoting Integrated Nutrient Management (INM), which advocates the judicious and scientific integration of organic sources, chemical fertilisers, and biological inputs for efficient and sustainable nutrient management,” the Ministry said adding that the INM aims to meet the nutrient requirements of crops in an economical and environmentally sustainable manner while maintaining long-term soil fertility. It had also experimented with Nano Urea, which is yet to get popularity among farmers, apparently after controversies over its scientific efficacy and result.

title: Farmers’ outfits urge MPs, MLAs to speak out against trade deals; seek scrapping of all FTAs

content.value: The Samyukt Kisan Morcha (SKM), a joint platform of about 500 farmers’ organisations, has written to all MPs and MLAs drawing their attention to the “deep agrarian, economic and social distress” confronting farmers and workers. SKM has urged people’s representatives to raise their voices against the proposed India-United States Free Trade Agreement (FTA), demanding that all FTAs be repealed.

Another key demand is the passage of an Act that ensures a minimum support price as recommended by the National Farmers Commission, headed by M. S. Swaminathan, with guaranteed procurement for all crops. The group demands a comprehensive loan waiver to end rural indebtedness and peasant and daily worker suicides along with ₹25 lakh compensation to the family of each peasant suicide victim. Other demands include scrapping of the four Labour Codes, a minimum wage of ₹ 31,000 for all workers, restoration of the MGNREGA mandating 200 days of work and ₹ 700 as a wage, withdrawal of the draft Electricity Bill, the Seeds Bill 2025, and the draft National Food Security Act.

“The FTAs are a blueprint for the economic colonisation of India. FTAs will allow the import of agri-products, further eroding agricultural viability, capturing the food processing markets, and changing cropping patterns, which will damage food self-reliance,” the memorandum added.

Alleging that a duopoly of Adani and Leap India had developed in the silos of the Food Corporation of India, the SKM said 77.5% of the grains will be controlled by the two companies. “We the farmers are committed to resist this corporate takeover of agriculture and will fight to protect India’s self-reliance and sovereignty,” it added.

title: YSRCP leader criticises government’s response to El Nino crisis in Anantapur

content.value: YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) Anantapur district president and former MLA Anantha Venkatarami Reddy has alleged that the State government had failed to implement necessary alternate measures to mitigate the El Nino impact.

Speaking to the media here on Sunday, the senior leader claimed that, according to initial expectations, the impact of El Niño would subside by August. However, scientists state that the present phenomenon is a ‘Super El Niño’ and will persist throughout the year, he added.

“The undivided Anantapur district is set to face an acute shortage of drinking water, irrigation water, and cattle fodder. Reduced crop cultivation during the previous Kharif season has already led to scarcity of fodder. Haystacks are not to be found in the villages, and livestock is already being moved to market yards,” he alleged.

Mr. Venkatarami Reddy said that Anantapur is the second district in the country with the lowest rainfall. “This region has previously suffered from severe droughts that left cattle emaciated, and the conditions appear to be heading in that direction again,” he claimed.

During this Kharif season, Anantapur district recorded a rainfall deficit of 45%, while Sri Sathya Sai district recorded a deficit of 53%. Crop cultivation was limited to just 55% of the land in Anantapur district and 45% in Sri Sathya Sai district, he claimed. Even the crops that were sown during the Kharif season are withering, with some areas reporting total crop failure due to drought.
While the district was supposed to receive 27 tmcft of water from the Tungabhadra Dam, reports indicate that only 16 tmcft will be allocated this year.

The senior leader claimed that currently 167 tmcft of water was available at the Srisailam reservoir, however, the authorities were failing to secure adequate water supplies for Rayalaseema region. “In the undivided Anantapur district, the Ministers, MPs, and MLAs all belong to the ruling party, but no one is paying attention to the water crisis or the state of the crops,” he said.

Mr. Venkatarami Reddy alleged that while Rayalaseema was facing a difficult situation, Telangana was diverting water. “If the current situation at Srisailam persists, the reservoir will run dry in another 10 days,” he said, and added that the public representatives from undivided Anantapur district must respond and meet the Chief Minister and demand release of more water for Rayalaseema.

title: Dharashiv MP pushes for crop loss survey and compensation for farmers in Marathwada region

content.value: Government of Maharashtra should survey crops that may have dried up due to inadequate rainfall said Dharashiv MP from Shiv Sena Omprakash Raje Nimbalkar. He demanded compensation and financial aid for the eligible farmers in the Marathwada region.

Mr. Nimbalkar sent a letter to Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde. In the letter, he said that there has been almost no rainfall in the region of Marathwada for the past 45 days. “The soybean crop has dried due to lack of water. Farmers have faced a financial loss due to this and are in trouble. The situation is serious, and surveys should be conducted through the revenue and agriculture departments to ascertain the losses. The farmers who have faced losses and are eligible should be given financial assistance,” he added.
The Marathwada region has faced a rainfall deficit since June 1. The region has so far received 381 mm (77%) average rainfall in all eight districts against the expected 498.8 mm.

The rainfall deficit in Dharashiv Lok Sabha constituency stood at 25.3%. Dharashiv district has received rainfall of 301.5 mm against the average expected rainfall of 403.5 mm, according to a revenue department report.

title: A global Centre of Excellence to come up in Coimbatore for research on sugarcane

content.value: A global Centre of Excellence (CoE) will come up at the Indian Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore, at ₹90 crore to develop new varieties of sugarcane.

Harshvardhan Patil, president of the National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories, told journalists in Coimbatore on Friday that the Union government is expected to provide ₹45 crore and the rest will come be contributed by the industry.
The investments will be made in the next four years.

“Sugar mills in the country used to operate for almost 200 days a year. Now, they operate for just 100 days in a year. Sugarcane production is declining because of pests, weather, high temperature, water logging, and so on. Development of a new variety takes almost 14 years. The Global Centre of Excellence for Accelerated Sugarcane Genetic Improvement that will come up in Coimbatore will develop new varieties in eight years,” he said.
The Union government, ICAR, ISMA, NFCSF, and the Institute will sign an agreement soon for setting up of the Centre.

The Centre of Excellence will work on developing new varieties that will have higher yield and sugar recovery, enhanced tolerance to drought, flood, salinity, and heat stress, improved resistance to major diseases and pests, better ratooning ability, and suitability for sugar, ethanol, bioenergy, and sustainable agriculture.

In Maharashtra, about two lakh sugarcane farmers are benefitting from the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Tamil Nadu government should look at supporting sugarcane farmers here in adopting AI, he added.

The Additional Director of the Directorate of Sugar, Tamil Nadu, S. Arunraj, said sugar production in the State this year was expected to be almost the same as last year. Nearly 1.31 lakh hectare was under sugarcane and the area was declining. While Tamil Nadu was the sixth largest sugar producing State in the country it had the highest productivity. With extreme heat in the sugarcane growing areas, sugar recovery was just about 8 %. The Centre that will come up in Coimbatore will develop new varieties that will give higher sugar recovery, he said.
A delegation from Tamil Nadu will visit Maharashtra to study the use of AI and introduce it here in the next few months, Mr. Arunraj said.
Prakash Naiknavare, Managing Director of the Federation, added that a delegation visited sugarcane farms and the facilities at the Institute.

According to the Director of the Sugarcane Breeding Institute, P. Govindaraj, the Centre will have trained personnel, world class infrastructure, and international collaborations to develop the required varieties of sugarcane.

title: Apong: Assam’s traditional rice wine is now bottled as Ti:Po

content.value: Japan has sake, Korea has makgeolli. India has Ti:Po, Po:Ro Apong. The traditional rice wine of the Mising community of Assam, apong is now a premium bottled drink. Apong, also popular in Assam as sai mod (ash liquor), is prepared from rice and uses foraged herbs. Ti:Po in Mising language means a satisfactory drink.

But unlike the cloudy makgeolli and crystal clear sake, Ti:Po is close to Bourbon whiskey in appearance. With 14% alcohol content, a sip of Ti:Po is closer to sake with two distinct ending notes — sweet and smoky. The other distinct notes are fruity and nutty.

The idea to present apong as a premium bottled drink (only available in Assam for now) lies with the founders Dipankar Kalita, Abhijit Pegu and singer and music composer, Joi Barua. However, it is common knowledge that bottling an indigenous drink to be sold in stores is not a simple task.

To be able to present Ti:Po as a premium beverage, the founders combined traditional Mising craftsmanship with patented modern technology. The company has patented the technology of removing microbes (that leads to spoilage) and multiple filtration.
All this while empowering local women with sustainable livelihoods.

Dipankar says, “Ti:Po stays true to the phrase ’it takes a village to raise a child’. Po:Ro Apong, the traditional, home-brewed rice beer, has cultural  significance for the Mising people of Assam. So, we couldn’t think of brewing it without the experts who have honed brewing skills from their ancestors.”

As the idea was conceptualised, the team worked with local women to keep the taste, technique and process authentic. Since home-brewed rice alcohol, like food, varies from household to household, they identified a group of women who would work as a team.

Abhijit Pegu, one of the three co-founders said, “Over a span of two years, we tasted and tried Apong from several households repeatedly to track consistency. This also included testing for preservation, acidity, sweetness, colour and smokiness. As we tasted, we kept filtering the group of households that were able to maintain the pre-decided requirements. We further filtered down to form a group of 20 women. Once this was sorted, we moved to the next step.” A group of 20 women can approximately produced 5,000 bottles of apong.

To preserve the tradition, Ti:Po also partnered with two Self Help Groups — Polo SHG (Laimekuri) and Aaradha SHG (Memberchuk). The women brewmasters remain custodians of the craft while becoming part of the supply chain.

The drink is unique because it derives its flavour from the herbs of Assam. “The State, endowed with rich and varied flora and fauna, is a living library of flavour. Ladies, who are expert herb collectors, pick over 60 forest botanicals, according to the season. “In the forest, each season begins with different herbs. The forest decides what is available. The collectors decide what should be taken and what should be left behind,” explained Dipankar.

A slight variation is embraced as a natural expression rather than corrected. The gathered botanicals are handed to the women brewmasters. This starter also does not impose flavour. It invites fermentation — recruiting native yeasts and microbes specific to the place.

Abhijit added, “Ti:po is special because it is handcrafted only by the women of Mising community and undergoes possibly world’s only solid state fermentation combining over 60 herbs and burnt rice husk giving it a unique smoky nutty and fruity profile.”

Explaining the process, Dipankar added, “The semi-cooked rice grains are first coated with e-pob (the starter prepared from the herbs), then with finely burnt husk. Each grain of rice then turns into a micro chamber of fermentation. The delicate boundary where rice, starter and husk meet is where alcohol develops, giving the drink its depth, texture and character. Every grain becomes its own cellar.”

Fermentation takes place in small batches of five to seven kilograms. Brewmasters keep track of the process by sight, scent and time instead of relying on automation. It is this painstakingly long process that makes scaling production not so easy. Joi says, “Everything depends on human judgement rather than machines. We have to be on constant watch. We are fine with small batches of perfect products.”
Once the fermentation is over, the drawing of the wine is carried out.
Technology only aids

Ti:Po’s role is to preserve Po:ro Apong using hygienic production, scientific filtration and clean bottling while maintaining its traditional character. The brand has a chief winemaker, Ajoy Shaw (DipWSET), who oversees the process.

Now that Ti:Po is ready, what does one pair it with? “It complements any Indian chakna by balancing spice, lifting aromatics and cleansing the palate. It pairs especially well with tandoori dishes, kebabs, smoked meats, pepper-forward recipes and savoury snacks.”
Ti:Po is priced at ₹1,800 and is only available in Assam for now.

title: Opium farmers demand more farming licences, ₹1 lakh per kg

content.value: Ahead of the announcement of the opium licensing policy for 2026-27, scheduled for September, opium farmers from Madhya Pradesh,Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have urged the Union Government to formulate it in a manner that benefits the country and farmers.

At a protest meeting in Jantar Mantar here on Monday (August 17, 2026), under the banner of Bharatiya Afeem Kisan Sangharsh Samiti, the licensee farmers said the number of opium licenses for medicinal opium cultivation should be increased, and the price of opium procured by the Government should be hiked to ₹1,00,000 per kg for farmers, in line with the international market price.
From 2023: Uncertain future in a sea of poppies

The farmers said in a representation to the Government that the opium leases that have been cancelled since 1990 should be reinstated, so that the cultivation of opium, which has increased significantly since 2008, can be further expanded. “Morphine content depends on natural factors and is not in the farmers’ control. Therefore, opium leases should be granted based on a morphine yield of three kgs per hectare,” they demanded.

The farmers said the poppy straws should be excluded from the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act and claimed that they are not a narcotic substance but rather the husk of the poppy plant. The farmers demanded that the Concentrate of Poppy Straw (CPS) method of opium harvest, which the Government has been promoting based on international experience since the 2021-22 crop year, should be completely abolished, and the traditional opium cultivation should be promoted. “The government should rather purchase poppy straws at a rate of ₹2,000 per kg and process them for upgrading their quality,” they added.

As per the 2025-26 policy, nearly 1.21 lakh farmers are estimated to be eligible for licenses to cultivate opium in these States. “This represents a 23.5% increase over the number of licenses actually issued in the previous crop year. The policy thus brings approximately 15,000 additional farmers into the fold, who are expected to benefit from opium cultivation this year,” the Government had said in September, 2025 while announcing the new policy.

“The Central Government continues to ensure adequate supply of alkaloids to meet medical and palliative care needs. Concurrently, efforts are underway to augment processing capacity through indigenous and self-reliant measures, with a view to meeting the requirements of alkaloids for the production of essential narcotic drugs,” it added.

title: Farmers’ union to mobilise one million ‘swayamsevaks’ to fight trade deals

content.value: The Samyukt Kisan Morcha (SKM), the umbrella organisation for about 500 farmers’ outfits, has decided to enrol one million young kisan swayamsevaks (farmer volunteers) to protest against bilateral and multilateral trade treaties the country has signed or proposes to sign with other countries. The organisation will hold kisan panchayats in one lakh villages in September and October to galvanise farmers against such free trade agreements (FTAs).

Talking to reporters here on Thursday (September 3, 2026), SKM leaders said delegations have met more than 100 Ministers, MPs, and MLAs across the country with a charter of demands that includes cancellation of all FTAs. They said they have also written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi seeking an audience. “The Prime Minister’s Office received our letter but has not yet given us an appointment. SKM believes the PM has become inaccessible to India’s farmers who are 65% of the population. It is shocking that the PM has shown no interest in meeting representatives of the vast majority of the people of India, and this shows the RSS-BJP combine’s lack of concern for farmers,” they said.

They said while withdrawing the year-long farmers’ protests in 2021, written assurances were given to the SKM, but none of those were fulfilled, including a farm loan waiver, and a legalised minimum support price. “SKM will hold Maha Panchayats in one lakh villages on October 3, 2026 — Lakhimpur Kheri Martyrs Day. A list of 10 lakh farmer volunteers, including 2.5 lakh women farmers, will then be issued to restart the farmers’ struggle from November 26, 2026,” they added.

“The National Council and General Body of the SKM will meet at Karnal, Haryana on October 12 and work out the details to restart the farmers’ struggle from November 26 if the Modi regime continues to neglect farmers’ demands ,” they said.

title: Don’t cultivate paddy this kharif, Andhra Pradesh tells Krishna delta farmers amid water crunch

content.value: The Andhra Pradesh government has appealed to farmers in the Krishna delta not to take up paddy cultivation during the kharif season, citing an unprecedented water shortage caused by delayed and inadequate rainfall under the influence of a Super El Niño-like weather pattern.

Addressing a press conference here on Friday (July 24, 2026), Engineer-in-Chief (Irrigation) K. Narasimha Murthy said water storage in the Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar reservoirs on the Krishna had fallen to critically low levels, the monsoon rains having failed to arrive on time. He said upstream reservoirs, including Almatti, Narayanpur and Jurala, still had around 50 TMC of vacant storage, indicating that substantial inflows into the downstream reservoirs were yet to materialise. In the prevailing conditions, any inflows reaching Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar would have to be given top priority for drinking water, he said.

Although the Pulichintala reservoir holds around 29 TMC of water, only about 25 TMC is usable. If the uncertainty in rainfall continues, this water may also have to be conserved to meet drinking water needs until June 2027, he said.

To meet the drinking water needs of the Krishna delta, the government is diverting Godavari water through the Polavaram Right Main Canal using the Pattiseema Lift Irrigation Scheme. However, inflows into the Godavari have also declined sharply, limiting the operation of the Pattiseema pumping system. All 24 pumps at Pattiseema cannot be operated because of the reduced river flows. Last week, water had to be supplemented from the Sileru, a measure that had never been required in the past. While the Pattiseema pumps earlier received sufficient water for 100 to 120 days each season, the present situation is expected to limit availability to about 60 to 70 days, Mr. Narasimha Murthy said, adding: “Supplying water to the Godavari delta ayacut remains the first priority before diverting water to other regions.”
With Godavari inflows declining, only 15 pumps at Pattiseema are working, releasing around 1,000 cusecs into the Polavaram Right Main Canal.

Mr. Narasimha expressed concern that some farmers along the Polavaram Right Main Canal were drawing water through unauthorised pumps, reducing the quantity reaching the Krishna delta canal system. This, officials said, was affecting the canal flows needed for drinking water supply.

He expressed concern that some farmers along the Polavaram Right Main Canal were drawing water through unauthorised pumps, reducing the quantity reaching the Krishna delta canal system. This, officials said, was affecting the canal flows needed for drinking water supply.

Mr. Narasimha cautioned that even if farmers used Pattiseema water now for raising paddy nurseries, they could face severe losses if Godavari inflows declined further and pumping was suspended in the coming weeks. If Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar received sufficient inflows beyond drinking water requirements, the Agriculture and Water Resources Departments would jointly prepare a scientific plan for kharif cultivation, Mr. Narasimha said.

Appealing for the cooperation of farmers, Mr. Narasimha asked them not to take up paddy cultivation in the present circumstances. He warned that without adequate reservoir storage, and if rainfall remained deficient, farmers risked losing their entire investment.
Farmers in the Krishna delta have instead been advised to opt for less water-intensive dry crops wherever feasible until the water situation improves, he added.

title: Despite 51% rainfall deficit, AP sustains kharif cultivation through advance planning: Atchannaidu

content.value: Agriculture and Fisheries Minister Kinjarapu Atchannaidu on Wednesday (August 26, 2026) said the Andhra Pradesh government had taken advance measures to protect kharif cultivation from the impact of severe rainfall deficit and El Niño conditions, claiming that its alternative cropping strategy had helped sustain agricultural activity across the State.

The Minister said Andhra Pradesh received only 192.8 mm of rainfall between the first week of June and August 25, against the normal 393.7 mm, recording a deficit of 51%. Despite the adverse conditions, kharif crops had been raised in 20.35 lakh hectares, he said.

Highlighting the shift towards less water-intensive crops, Mr. Atchannaidu said the area under pulses increased by 23.6%, from 2.16 lakh hectares by August 25 last year to 2.66 lakh hectares this year. The area under red gram rose from 1.92 lakh hectares to 2.30 lakh hectares, while black gram increased from 17,000 hectares to 30,000 hectares. Green gram and soybean also registered higher acreage.

Paddy continued to occupy the largest area at 10.37 lakh hectares, followed by red gram at 2.30 lakh hectares, groundnut at 1.37 lakh hectares and maize at one lakh hectares. Cotton acreage remained broadly stable at 3.97 lakh hectares, marginally higher than 3.96 lakh hectares last year.

The Minister said the government had begun preparing for a possible El Niño impact as early as February after receiving alerts from the Centre. District-wise drought mitigation and contingency plans were drawn up, particularly for Rayalaseema, Prakasam and Markapuram regions, with emphasis on promoting crops requiring less water.
He said the State had been implementing the “Raithanna Meekosam – El Niño Impact Mitigation Plan – Kharif 2026” programme across Andhra Pradesh since August 7.

Mr. Atchannaidu also highlighted a sharp expansion in crop insurance coverage. Insurance applications increased from 19.5 lakh in Kharif 2025 to 35.1 lakh in Kharif 2026, while the insured area rose from 7.83 lakh hectares to 15.1 lakh hectares—an increase of about 108%.

The number of applications from non-loanee farmers increased from about two lakh to 20.35 lakh, he said, adding that crops valued at around ₹13,983 crore had so far been brought under insurance coverage. Farmers enrolled under the voluntary insurance system pay only 2% of the premium, with the remaining amount shared by the Centre and the State, according to the Minister.

Launching a political attack on former Chief Minister Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy, Mr. Atchannaidu alleged that the previous YSRCP government had failed to provide adequate crop insurance protection and had left premium dues of around ₹2,000 crore.

He said the present government had submitted a roadmap to the Centre for clearing the pending liabilities and had allocated ₹250 crore in the 2026-27 budget estimates, while also releasing the required premium amount into an escrow account to facilitate smooth registration of farmers for Kharif 2026.
“The coalition government’s objective is to ensure crop insurance protection and financial security for farmers’ families, particularly during adverse weather conditions,” the Minister said.

title: Govt. appeals to farmers not to use canal water for irrigation

content.value: The district administration has appealed to farmers not to use canal water for irrigation and use water judiciously.

As many as seven of the 15 taluks have received normal rainfall but the rest have received scanty rains. Overall, the district has 20% rainfall deficit. Compared to last year, the water storage in Hidkal and Navilutirtha reservoirs is less this year.
The government has instructed to use the available water for drinking purposes until next summer, Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Roshan said here on Friday.

“Some people are demanding to release water into the canals for feeding the crops. However, for now, we have planned to use the water for drinking purposes only. We will try to release water for agriculture if more water flows into the reservoirs in the coming days,” he told reporters.
Meanwhile, due to reduced rainfall in parts of Maharashtra and Belagavi district, there was a slight reduction in the discharge from the neighbouring State.
On Friday, the discharge from Maharashtra stood at 89,442 cusecs, around 208 cusecs less than that on Thursday.
The Almatti dam had an inflow of around 84,611 cusecs and outflow of 67,500 cusecs. Live storage was around 89.3 tmcft against the full capacity of 123 tmcft.
The inflow into the Hipparagi Barrage was around 69,700 cusecs and outflow was 69,050 cusecs.

title: Scattered rains renew farmers’ hope for a better yield in Yadgir district

content.value: Yadgir district, which had registered a deficit rainfall, has got some hopes back for a good yield after experiencing scattered rains a couple of days back.
The district has recorded 2,41,682 hectares of sowing till Friday, against its targeted area of 4,01,869 for the Kharif season.

Out of the 84,999 hectares, the redgram covered 48,697 ( 60.14%) hectares, the greengram covered 9,153 hectares against the targeted area of 13,770 hectares, while the cotton was sown on 1,79,410 hectares against the targeted area of 2,02,452 hectares.

In the wake of deficit rainfall this monsoon, crops like cotton, redgram and greengram had begun to wither due to a shortage of rain and moisture. The wait by the farmers for a good spell of rain seems to have ended with the scattered rains for a couple of days.
Farmer Vijay Gulgi is now a bit relieved that they have received scattered rainfall which they believe is going to help the standing crops.

After paddy, cotton is the second largest grown crop in the district and the farmers are dependent on water that is made available through irrigation. However, considering the drought condition, district administration had announced that the water available at Basavasagar Reservoir should be used only for human and animal drinking purposes and not for irrigation.

Farmers like Chandrashekhar Gouda Bilwar, who cultivate cotton, are dependent on the canal water made available through Krishna Bhagya Jala Nigama Limited (KBJNL). “But because of dry spell, the crops started withering after the first round of weed-removing activities was completed. The recent scattered rains somehow help the withering crops. Now, I am confident again about getting a good yield instead of expected crop loss,” he said.
According to data, the district has suffered a 24% rain deficit that was recorded from June 1 to July 24.

title: Direct Karnataka to release backlog of 17.604 tmcft Cauvery water: T.N. to Supreme Court

content.value: The Tamil Nadu government approached the Supreme Court on Sunday (August 30, 2026), seeking a direction to Karnataka to release 17.604 tmcft of water from the Cauvery River, the balance quantity as of August 27, based on the pro-rata formula.

The State, in a supplementary affidavit settled by senior advocate G. Umapathy and re-settled by C.S. Vaidyanathan, also urged the court to order Karnataka to release 9,000 cusecs of water between August 26 and September 8, as directed by the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) in its 56th meeting.

It further sought the top court’s intervention to direct Karnataka to make good the shortfall between the flows ensured at Billigundulu, a riverside village on the border between the two States, and the flows that the CWMA had directed to take place between August 27 and August 30.
‘Farmers severely affected’

“Ground reality is that the Cauvery Basin of Tamil Nadu is very severely affected. The farmers of the Cauvery Delta are seriously prejudiced, as the Kuruvai season is almost over and Mettur could not be open for irrigation for want of adequate storage and cultivation of the samba crop and has been severely affected, which is causing great anxiety amongst the farming community in the Cauvery Delta as they are not getting the due share even on a pro-rata basis in the current water year,” Tamil Nadu submitted, in the affidavit filed by advocate B. Karunakaran.
A Bench headed by Justice Vikram Nath is scheduled to hear the Cauvery case on August 31.

The previous hearing on August 24 had witnessed the top court advising Tamil Nadu to voice its concern about the release of the “proportionate” quantity of Cauvery water due from Karnataka before the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) and the CWMA, in meetings scheduled during the week.
‘Raised concerns to CWRC’

Tamil Nadu said that its member, in a CWRC meeting held on August 24, had raised the State’s entitlement to receive around 28 TMC. The member had asked the CWRC to facilitate the release of around 22,000 cusecs (1.9 TMC per day) for 15 days, starting from August 24.

The State had also submitted before the CWRC that Karnataka had already drawn over 20 TMC from its canals for irrigation and also through anicut channels and lift irrigation systems, while Tamil Nadu had till date not been able to open the Mettur reservoir for irrigation.

“However, CWRC directed Karnataka to ensure releases from its reservoirs so that the flows at the rate of 9,000 cusecs are realised at Billigundulu with effect from August 25 till September 8,” Tamil Nadu said.
It said that CWRC had fixed 9,000 cusecs for the next 15 days with effect from August 25, without considering the accumulated backlog of 17.415 TMC as of August 23.
‘Backlog must be released’
Tamil Nadu said it had raised its grievance before the CWMA, at its meeting the very next day on August 25, about the “gross inadequacy” of the CWRC order for release of Cauvery water.

The State informed the top court that it had urged the CWMA to direct Karnataka to ensure the release of 1.9 TMC per day from August 24 to September 7 to ensure that the backlog in terms of the pro-rata formula is also released by Karnataka.

“However, CWMA, without considering the purport of the scheme framed under Section 6A of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which mandates pro-rata releases in the distress years, scrupulously failed to take any steps to direct Karnataka to make good the same. CWMA mechanically affirmed the recommendation of CWRC and directed Karnataka to ensure only 9,000 cusecs per day from August 25 to September 8,” the Tamil Nadu affidavit said.

title: India’s rice fields now rank among world’s top methane hotspots

content.value: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from paddy fields worldwide have doubled since the 1960s, a new study in NatureFood has found. In the most recent decade, 2011-2020, paddy fields around the world produced around 1.1 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent (CO2-e) emissions every year — a 90.4% increase from the annual emissions between 1961 and 1980, the study reported.

Upon examining the sources contributing to the rise in emissions, the study found that about half the increase was driven by the loss of soil organic carbon. Between 1961 and 1980, paddy fields were soil organic carbon sinks, removing some 289 million tonnes of CO2-e emissions annually. However, the sink weakened over time. In the 2010s, over a third of paddy fields worldwide in fact began losing carbon from the soil.

title: Livelihood initiative launched for Nagaland prisoners

content.value: The Phek district police in Nagaland have launched ‘Project Revive’ to improve the lives of inmates at the district jail, initiated on July 25. Phek, located near the borders of Manipur and Myanmar, is about 110 km east of Kohima, the state capital.
A brainchild of the district’s Superintendent of Police, Pritpal Kaur, the initiative aims to provide livelihood training to the prisoners. The Phek district jail currently has 23 male inmates.
The district police collaborated with the Krishi Vigyan Kendra-Indian Council of Agricultural Research (KVK-ICAR) and the District Legal Services Authority in Phek town for the project.

“The training programme is envisaged to aid in the rehabilitation of the inmates, enabling them to earn an honest living after overcoming past mistakes and temptations,” Dr. Kaur, a dentist-turned-IPS officer, said on Wednesday (July 29, 2026).
During the launch programme, she encouraged the jail inmates to transform their lives with “revived hearts” and contribute to a peaceful and progressive society.

Sanjeev Kumar Singh, a Senior Scientist and head of KVK-ICAR’s Phek centre, highlighted the significance of the project and outlined upcoming agricultural initiatives. He said the centre plans to provide red cauliflower seeds to the inmates so they can cultivate the vegetables within the jail premises.
He also said that T. Esther Longkumer, Phek KVK-ICAR’s Chief Technical Officer (Soil Science), has been training the inmates on vermicomposting and other sustainable livelihood skills.

Dr. Kaur said the second phase of the training will focus on handicrafts, including cane stools, furniture, and other vocational skills. “The district police will engage another team for the second phase,” she said.
She said ‘Project Revive’ has a marketing plan factored in. The products made by the prisoners will be sold in the markets of Kohima and Dimapur, Nagaland’s commercial hub.
The profits earned will be shared among the inmates and deposited into their bank accounts.

The launch event, chaired by Nukhochiyi Tetseo, Jailor of Phek District Jail, concluded with practical hands-on training and a motivational address encouraging inmates to pursue hard work and lead purposeful living, marking a significant step in the rehabilitation of prisoners.

title: Where have Bengaluru’s signature fruits gone?

content.value: Ramachandra Gowda, 60, rides his moped every day from home to his two-acre vineyard in Bettahalasur, about 25 km north of Bengaluru. Once upon a time, Bettahalasur had acres of vineyards, besides fields yielding a variety of vegetables and betel leaves.
The likes of Gowda are now few, as the city has expanded. Most farmers on the outskirts have moved away from farming and agricultural land has been replaced by thousands of multi-storey buildings.

title: They crossed the State border for healthcare. Now, Andhra Pradesh is helping this Telangana hospital

content.value: After 52 patients from Andhra Pradesh were rushed to Bhadrachalam Area Hospital in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem district during an overnight medical emergency, the Polavaram district administration offered to support the Telangana hospital with medicines and drugs, recognising that nearly 40% of its patient load comes from Andhra Pradesh.

The 52 patients, including 47 children and five adults, were brought to the hospital from Gollaguppa village in Polavaram district, Andhra Pradesh, after reportedly falling ill post taking chloroquine tablets distributed during a health camp. One child was brought dead, while 12 patients tested positive for malaria.

A large number of children and adults arrived at the facility within a short period, but the hospital did not turn away patients from across the border. Despite having limited staff initially available, Bhadradri Kothagudem District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS) G. Ravi Babu and Area Hospital Superintendent Rajasekhar Reddy and the hospital team immediately mobilised additional doctors and support staff who worked through the night, initiating treatment and closely monitoring the children and adults.
Polavaram District Collector K. Dinesh Kumar appreciated the Bhadrachalam Area Hospital team for extending immediate, compassionate and professional care to patients from Andhra Pradesh.

But the response from Andhra Pradesh went beyond appreciation. The Polavaram district administration assured that medicines required by Bhadrachalam Area Hospital would be extended to the facility. Nearly 40% of its patient load comes from Andhra Pradesh, making the Bhadrachalam facility an important healthcare centre for people living in neighbouring areas of the State.

Dr. G. Ravi Babu said the incident demonstrated the strength and responsiveness of a well-coordinated public healthcare system. “For a healthcare professional, a patient’s identity is never defined by State boundaries,” he said.

title: Bhutan leads South-East Asia in eliminating rabies as public health problem

content.value: Bhutan has become the first country in the World Health Organization’s South-East Asia Region to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies as a public health problem. The WHO, on Saturday, validated Bhutan’s achievement. The mountain kingdom’s last rabies death was in June 2023.
Rabies burden

Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal if clinical symptoms appear. It is estimated that rabies still claims the lives of approximately 59,000 people each year, with a third of these fatalities occurring in India, where it remains a huge problem with local bodies failing at animal birth control and vaccination programmes.

The disease is endemic throughout the country except for the Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands, and cases are reported from all over the country, the year round. About 96% of the mortality and morbidity is associated with dog bites.The National Rabies Control Programme aims to reduce mortality from rabies among human beings and progressively achieve the target of bringing rabies deaths to zero by 2030.

In a  message shared on the WHO website, its Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus congratulated Bhutan ‘which is another step towards our goal to end human deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030.’ He further noted the interventions that made the success possible: “Bhutan’s success shows that the health of humans, animals and the environment we share is inextricably linked. By uniting health workers, veterinarians, and communities, Bhutan has shown that the fight against rabies is won not in silos, but through solidarity across all sectors.”

WHO validation recognises that a country has eliminated dog-transmitted human rabies and consequently through the absence of human deaths from the disease for at least two years, while demonstrating the capacity to prevent transmission from re-emerging. This criterion was set out by the WHO Expert Consultation on Rabies in 2018.
Preventing transmission

Rabies deaths are preventable. A two-pronged strategy is advocated globally- vaccinating dogs to curb the disease at source, and using post exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after a bite. PEP consists of thoroughly washing the bite area with water and soap, administering a full course of human rabies vaccine and, whenever necessary, rabies immunoglobulins.

The WHO attributes the One Health approach, or the firm belief that human and animal health are intrinsically like to ecosystems, to Bhutan’s success story. “Through this approach, Bhutan has prioritised resource allocation, integrated surveillance, and strategic planning,” a WHO statement has recorded. When a suspected rabies case is reported, animal and human health authorities collaborate to identify potential exposures and conduct joint field investigations under the One Health framework.

Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region, complimented the country: “The dedication of health workers, veterinary professionals and De-suung volunteers known as ‘Guardians of Peace’ helped take dog vaccination, population management and community awareness to every part of the country.”
Sustaining rabies control

A strong collaboration was initiated between the Ministries of Health and the Agriculture and Livestock, together with partners, local governments and communities, united through a One Health approach, Bhutan’s health ministry sources explained. Continued access to PEP, mass dog vaccination, dog population management, community engagement and strengthened surveillance marked the country’s programme.

Bhutan will reportedly continue to maintain the systems that underpin this achievement. Its Nationwide Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme will be sustained with the same vigour, according to the WHO. Cross-border coordination with adjacent Indian states will be further strengthened to safeguard this success in rabies control.

title: Taking a leaf out of Amul’s textbook to help rare-disease patients

content.value: Patient data, including medical records and patient experiences, are essential for scientists to develop new treatments, especially for rare diseases. The data help identify diagnostic biomarkers, predict disease progression, and help investigators design better clinical trials.

This is important because clinical trials are required to show that a new treatment is safe and effective before a country’s regulators approve it. Conventional clinical trials involve a large number of participants and include both treatment and control groups. However, for rare diseases, too few people are eligible to participate, and it is not possible to have a control group.

In these situations, patient registries and natural-history studies can provide real-world data that can serve as ‘external’ controls. Natural-history studies record clinical parameters, including those reported by patients, over time, allowing clinicians to model disease progression in the absence of treatments. Patient data can also help scientists identify suitable participants and meaningful clinical endpoints to properly evaluate complicated treatments.

Thus, by improving trial design and reducing uncertainty, comprehensive patient datasets can help researchers develop drugs faster, increase the chances of their receiving regulatory approval, and ultimately help bring safe and effective treatments to patients with rare diseases more quickly.
Patient data collective

For example, patient information collected over many years helped doctors understand how spinal muscular atrophy — a rare genetic condition that damages the spinal cord — progresses, identify the best ways to measure improvement, design good clinical trials, prove treatments work, and show that treating patients early gives the best results.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) models now make these goals possible in new ways — provided good patient data are available. Researchers can collect this data in two steps: first, create a community of patients with a given condition; and second, collect a range of medical and diagnostic records for those patients.

To implement this, the authors propose a cooperative model to create a ‘Patient Data Collective’ (PDC). The inspiration comes from the dairy cooperative Amul, which serves lakhs of farmers in India and ploughs back most of the profits from milk and milk-derived products to them. Amul also offers veterinary care and at-cost feed for cattle.

Similarly, a PDC for rare diseases in India can serve as a cooperative that holds patients’ data on their behalf to facilitate research, and which returns most, if any, of the revenue back to them. And the PDC can act on behalf of patients just as Amul does on behalf of farmers. It will access data from patient advocacy groups, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Health Mission, hospital records, the Centres of Excellence for Rare Diseases, clinicians, and other repositories.

In addition to its centralised repository, the PDC could have AI-based data analytics, with safeguards in place. That is, once a patient is registered, their consent to have their data collected, stored, analysed, and, indeed, protected.

Worldwide, patient advocacy groups are already helping research communities accelerate the development of drugs for rare diseases and navigate the approval ecosystem. This movement has also reached India, and active disease-specific groups could play a critical role in setting up and operating the PDC as well.
Setting up a collective

The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has already set up a rare disease registry based on data uploaded by a few experts from 19 specialised hospitals. The registry has collected data on around 4,000 patients with select diseases over the last five years.

Valuable though this resource is, it is also minuscule compared to India’s population. Given Indians’ experience with public registries, the data collection exercise behind the PDC should be flexible and inclusive, while maintaining accuracy and abiding by the highest ethical and legal standards.

This, in turn, is possible only as a patient-centric initiative with support from non-governmental organisations. Although setting up the proposed portal and backend database to accept data from all stakeholders while adhering to standards about accuracy, ethics, safety, and legality will be difficult, it is feasible, as demonstrated by the Citizen Health Platform operating in the U.S.

Once the portal is set up, patient data will need to be made easily available to the PDC through digital health records maintained by both public and private health providers. To aggregate scattered medical histories, genetic reports, and clinical notes, India can leverage its Ayushman Bharat Digital Health Mission: to mandate a clear governance model for a specialised, secure digital health locker or for the PDC to maintain patient records as such a locker.

Alongside a data repository, generative AI can be used as a tool to synthesise from large volumes of medical records medically relevant patterns that can inform doctors’ and patients’ decisions. Indeed, if an AI model is trained to engage with users in their local language, it can help analyse medical information to suggest possible diagnoses and lay out the various options, and thus encourage participation from diverse groups of patients.
Attracting drug developers
Support from the government or philanthropic organisations is needed to develop a platform with such AI capabilities, with clear governance and oversight.

In fact, the PDC should deliberately attempt to generate useful data. The authors suggest encouraging natural-history registries led by patient advocacy groups to generate longitudinal real-world evidence datasets. The groups can be funded to initiate natural history studies for their target diseases, with the data then channelled to the PDC.

Aggregating granular, everyday patient-reported metrics across India’s unique, genetically diverse endogamous populations could also attract drug developers from abroad seeking ethnically specific target-validation cohorts.

With recent updates to India’s New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, which embrace advanced computational modelling and non-animal testing models, Indian biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies can use the PDC to rapidly pre-screen and construct virtual synthetic control groups, making small-batch orphan drug evaluation clinically and financially viable within domestic budgets.

Just as Amul and the other cooperatives it inspired made India milk-secure and secured the livelihoods of millions of farmers, so too would a PDC have an outsized impact on drug discovery for most rare diseases, contributing to the good health of many patients who currently have few treatment options.
Alok Bhattacharya is an honorary visiting professor at the Tata Institute for Genetics and Society, Bengaluru. Gayatri Saberwal is a consultant at the Institute.

title: All you need to know about: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)

content.value: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of leukemia or blood cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow (spongy tissue inside the bones that forms blood cells). It is one of the lesser-known types of blood cancers in India. . According to a 2025 paper published in the  European Society of Medicine, CLL is one of the least common leukemias in India, accounting for less than 5% of all leukemias, with incidence rates ten times lesser than in the United States.
What is CLL?

The term ‘lymphocytic’ refers to the particular cells that are affected by this type of leukemia. In this condition the lymphocytes or group of white blood cells in the body exceed the normal count and increase in abnormal quantities inside the patient’s body.

The white blood cells form part of the immune system and help the body  fight diseases. When the body contracts an infection, the white blood cell count increases, in a defence mechanism to fight against the infection. As the infection gets better,  the white blood cell count decreases.  But when a person has CLL, the number of white blood cells do not subside even after an infection leaves the body.

CLL has a slower prognosis in the human body than other types of leukemia. According to doctors, CLL does not have any specific cause. . Doctors said most cases of CLL are not linked to environmental exposure, and are believed to arise from inherent oncogenic changes.
How is CLL diagnosed?

According to Aseem Kumar Samar, director - medical oncology, C.K. Birla Hospitals Jaipur,  CLL is a type of cancer that is sometimes discovered by chance during a regular blood check, in particular if lymphocyte counts are abnormally high. To diagnose this condition a complete blood count and a peripheral blood film (smear) are the first steps. Blood cell analysis by flow cytometry is key to confirm  the disease as this test reveals the typical abnormal B-lymphocytes present in CLL. “Based on the individual situation, other tests, for example, fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), TP53 mutation analysis  and immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable region (IGHV) testing -- all genetic tests -- will be done to understand the disease better, make plans and give a prognosis. In some cases doctors may ask for CT scans,” Dr. Samar added.
According to experts,  a bone marrow test is usually not a must for a proper diagnosis, but it can be done if there are certain reasons to justify it or if the doctor deems fit.
Symptoms and prognosis

CLL is usually asymptomatic initially, and presents  an increased lymphocyte count, according to Rajib De, head – clinical haematology, haemato-oncology & BMT, Manipal Hospital, EM Bypass, Kolkata.  “As the disease progresses, patients may develop swollen lymph nodes, weakness, weight loss and fever, followed in later stages by anaemia and low platelet counts,” Dr. De said.

CLL is broadly classified into Stage A, B and C, with Stage A being asymptomatic, Stage B involving lymph node swelling, and Stage C presenting with symptoms such as weakness, anemia and low platelets.
Treatment for CLL

Treatment for CLL depends on the stage of disease, symptoms, overall health, and specific genetic and molecular characteristics. Many patients with early, asymptomatic CLL do not require immediate treatment and can be safely monitored with a ‘watch and wait’ policy and regular blood tests and clinical evaluations.

Subhasish Chatterjee, who was diagnosed five years ago, said he has not been under any treatment. He only has regular checkups at the Tata Medical Centre - Cancer Hospital & Research Center in Kolkata. “I do blood tests and visit the doctor every six months, and I take a flu vaccine every year in March as a precautionary measure against infections, as was prescribed by the doctors. The doctor has not suggested any other treatment till my blood parameters remain the same,” said the 62-year-old. Mr Chatterjee was detected with CLL incidentally, after going for a check-up following a bout of Covid-19 in 2021.

When treatment becomes necessary, targeted oral therapies such as BTK inhibitors and BCL2 inhibitors, sometimes combined with anti-CD20 antibodies, are commonly used. The choice of therapy is increasingly guided by molecular markers such as TP53 abnormalities. Treatment is individualised, with the goal of controlling the disease effectively while maintaining quality of life and minimising treatment-related side effects, Dr. Samar said.

title: Maharashtra Bill does not regulate private hospital treatment rates, says health right group

content.value: Maharashtra Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill (CEB) has no provision to regulate treatment rates charged by private hospitals to patients, highlighted Jan Arogya Abhiyan (JAA), a coalition of NGOs and health professionals, on Friday while launching a statewide campaign appealing public to send objections to Joint Legislative Committee (JLC).

JLC is a committee comprising 21 MLAs, who have been reviewing the objections and suggestions on the Bill. The campaign also includes meetings with all 21 MLAs who are members of the JLC, demanding Health Minister convene a statewide consultation with organisations and networks working in the health sector to discuss the Bill.

JAA pointed out that the Bill must include fixed treatment charges for common procedures, different categories of beds, investigations, ICU services and doctors’ consultations; hospitals violating these rates should face penalties, a refund provision, a mandatory estimated bill by hospital detailing the treatment cost to be given to the patient, and the prescribed limit should not exceed estimated limit more than 5–10%.

The other suggested provision includes, ban withholding of patients or dead bodies over payment issues, establish accessible grievance-redressal system, establish an independent, well staffed regulatory authority, and ensure participation of all stakeholders in the State Council.

CEB was introduced in state Assembly on July 3, advocating compulsory registration of hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic centres transparency in treatment prices, and no deposit mandate for emergency cases. The new bill replaces the 77-years-old Maharashtra Nursing Homes Registration Act, 1949.

According to Arogya Abhiyan representatives, the analysis of hospital data from five major private hospitals in Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur shows that the average treatment charges faced by patients in these hospitals range from ₹24,000 to ₹62,000 per day. “This means just one day’s treatment in a large private hospital can cost as much as the average monthly per-capita income of a person in state,” said Abhay Shukla, the public health expert.

The latest NSS 80th Round data for Maharashtra shows as many as 77% of all hospitalisations in Maharashtra take place in private hospitals, highest among all states in India, average out-of-pocket expenditure on hospitalisation is ₹40,500, and on average rural hospitalisation costs have increased by 87%. 40 lakh people in Maharashtra are estimated to be pushed into poverty because of healthcare expenses.

Jan Arogya Abhiyan appealed to the Joint Legislative Committee to substantially strengthen this Bill in public interest as Section 11-Q of the Maharashtra Nursing Home Registration Act Rules, 2021 states that treatments rates should not exceed rates determined by the government.

title: Robert Bárány’s Nobel-winning discovery that transformed the understanding of balance and vertigo

content.value: The 1914 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Robert Bárány “for his work on the physiology and pathology of the vestibular apparatus.” His research established how the inner ear helps the body maintain balance and orientation, transforming the diagnosis of vertigo and disorders of equilibrium. Although the prize was awarded for 1914, Bárány received it in 1915 because the Nobel Committee had reserved the award for a year under its statutes.

At the turn of the twentieth century, physicians frequently encountered patients with dizziness, loss of balance, abnormal eye movements and unexplained sensations of spinning. While anatomists knew that structures within the inner ear were involved in equilibrium, the precise mechanisms remained poorly understood. There were few reliable methods to determine whether symptoms originated in the inner ear, the brain or the nervous system, making diagnosis difficult and treatment uncertain.
Early life

Robert Bárány was born on April 22, 1876, in Vienna, then part of Austria-Hungary. He studied medicine at the University of Vienna and developed a particular interest in neurological and ear disorders. After completing his medical training, he joined the Otological Clinic in Vienna under the renowned physician Adam Politzer. There, Bárány became fascinated by the relationship between the inner ear, balance and eye movements.

At the time he believed, from his early clinical observations that the vestibular apparatus, a system of fluid-filled canals and sensory organs within the inner ear, played a central role in maintaining equilibrium. He began investigating how disturbances in this system produced vertigo and other symptoms commonly seen in patients.
Bárány’s major contribution

Bárány’s breakthrough came through experiments involving the semicircular canals of the inner ear. While examining patients, he observed that introducing warm or cold water into the ear canal produced predictable eye movements known as nystagmus, along with sensations of motion and dizziness.

He demonstrated that temperature changes caused movement of fluid within the semicircular canals, stimulating the vestibular system and triggering characteristic responses. Cold water produced eye movements in one direction, while warm water produced movements in the opposite direction. These findings provided a practical way to assess the function of the balance organs of the inner ear.

Bárány’s work offered the first reliable physiological explanation for many forms of vertigo and established objective methods for evaluating vestibular disorders. The caloric test he developed became a cornerstone of neuro-otological examination and remains, in modified forms, part of vestibular assessment today.
Research contributions

Beyond identifying the effects of temperature on the vestibular apparatus, Bárány devised clinical tests that helped physicians distinguish disorders of the inner ear from neurological diseases affecting the brain and cerebellum. His investigations clarified how vestibular signals influence eye movements, posture and muscle tone.

These discoveries deepened understanding of the complex interactions between the inner ear, nervous system and motor control. They also provided clinicians with practical diagnostic tools that could be used at the bedside, making vestibular medicine a more precise scientific discipline.

Bárány’s research opened new avenues for studying balance disorders, motion sickness and neurological conditions that affect spatial orientation. His work also stimulated further investigations into the vestibular system, leading to advances in audiology, otology and neuroscience.
Impact on medicine

Today, disorders of balance and dizziness account for millions of medical consultations worldwide. Modern vestibular testing, including caloric stimulation and other assessments derived from Bárány’s principles, continues to play a central role in diagnosing conditions such as vestibular neuritis, Ménière’s disease and other inner-ear disorders.

His discoveries changed vertigo from a poorly understood symptom into a measurable physiological phenomenon. By demonstrating how the vestibular apparatus functions in health and disease, Bárány provided clinicians with tools that remain relevant more than a century later. His work also contributed to broader understanding of sensory integration and motor control within the nervous system.

When the First World War broke out, Bárány served as a surgeon in the Austrian army and was later captured as a prisoner of war in Russia. Remarkably, news of his Nobel Prize reached him while he was in captivity. Following international efforts, he was released and later accepted the prize. He subsequently joined Uppsala University in Sweden, where he continued his scientific work until his death on April 8, 1936.

Robert Bárány’s legacy endures in every modern clinic that evaluates dizziness, balance disorders or vestibular dysfunction. His meticulous investigations transformed understanding of one of the body’s most complex sensory systems and established principles that continue to guide medical practice today.

title: U.S. study tests psilocybin to fight cancer side effects

content.value: Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.

The study published Thursday in the journal Science involved tests on rats and certain human tissues as researchers looked at using psilocybin to fight a condition called peripheral neuropathy, which affects millions of people around the world.

It is a nerve ailment that hits about three quarters of all people who undergo chemo and commonly causes numbness and tingling, Patrick Dougherty, a co-author of the study, said in a call with reporters.
But a third of that group will develop non-stop, burning pain, said Dougherty, a pain treatment specialist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
The symptoms can lead to trouble walking and other debilitating complications that can last after a person finishes chemotherapy, and even remain with them for life.

And it is not just a quality-of-life issue. This complication also affects a cancer patient's chances of survival because sometimes the side effects are so bad they force doctors to cut back on chemo or stop it altogether.
Protecting nerves
It was almost by accident that these researchers found that psilocybin can help cancer patients.
The team was initially studying how the disease manages to hijack nerve cells in order to grow.

And the researchers were surprised to see the mushroom ingredient -- it was being used to study a brain pathway regeneration concept called neuroplasticity -- actually prevented the emergence of peripheral neuropathy.
Later experiments highlighted psilocybin's role in protecting nerve cells and stimulating inside them the transport of mitochondria, often referred to as a cell's powerhouse.
This is key because chemo destroys the microscopic railroads that allow mitochondria to send energy all the way to the tips of people's hands and feet, killing off nerve endings there.
Psilocybin also seems to act on the brain, preserving electrical activity that chemotherapy thwarts.

In rodents, taking two doses of psilocybin before chemo was enough to prevent the appearance of painful hypersensitivity during as many as six rounds of treatment. And it did this without affecting the animal's immune system or hindering the cancer-fighting action.
Careful with self-medicating
"This is a highly promising finding," said Kristy Townsend, a professor of neurobiology at The Ohio State University who was not involved in the study.
And psilocybin's nerve-protecting quality does not seem to be linked to its hallucinogenic effects because a non-hallucinogenic analogue had the same effect in a lab test, she added.
Before the treatment can be made standard for people, testing will be needed to see if it is safe and effective, said Townsend.

This will be a long, slow process though it should be eased by a boom in medical research on psychedelic substances and a Trump administration executive order in April to speed up research and regulatory reviews, these scientists say.
The MD Anderson Cancer Center plans to launch clinical tests with psilocybin on cancer patients later this year.
Meanwhile it is important for cancer patients to avoid using magic mushrooms on their own as treatment, the researchers warned.
Psilocybin is legal in a few U.S. states.

The drug has an "amplifier" effect and cancer patients who take it without supervision could feel more stressed and anxious than they already are because of their cancer diagnosis, said Gregory Jones, a psychiatrist who took part in the study released Thursday.
"If you put somebody in adversity under these psychedelic substances, you can get much worse," Jones said.

title: Eye donation in India: current scenario and way forward

content.value: Eye donation is said to be one of the most meaningful forms of donation, as a single donor can potentially restore sight to two individuals through corneal transplantation. India has made considerable progress in eye banking; the country currently has 396 functional eye banks, and corneal collections increased from 62,370 in 2022–23 to 69,848 in 2024–25. However, the need for donor tissue substantially exceeds its availability. There are approximately  2 million corneally blind people in our country, but only  40,000 corneal transplants performed per year.
Role of stakeholders

The government has a crucial role in strengthening the eye donation ecosystem through the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). Government support includes funding for eye bank infrastructure and equipment, training of ophthalmologists and eye bank technicians, promotion of eye donation, and provision of corneal storage media. Government hospitals can further improve donation rates by establishing Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes (HCRP) and integrating eye donation into routine end-of-life counselling.

Non-governmental organisations and service organisations have an equally important role in creating awareness, dispelling myths, encouraging pledges and, most importantly, counselling families at the time of death. Organisations such as eye bank networks, Lions Clubs and other community-based groups can take the message of eye donation to schools, colleges, workplaces and rural communities.

Private eye hospitals and institutions can complement these efforts by establishing or strengthening eye banks, developing efficient corneal retrieval networks, maintaining high standards of tissue evaluation and preservation, and providing advanced corneal transplantation. Recent initiatives such as the expansion of the National Eye Bank at AIIMS, Delhi through partnerships with additional hospitals demonstrate the value of collaborative retrieval networks.
Building strong PPPs

Ultimately, the future of eye donation in India lies in a strong public–private–NGO partnership. Awareness must translate into timely family consent, consent into retrieval, and retrieved tissue into high-quality transplantation. Strengthening this entire chain will be essential to bring down  the burden of corneal blindness and make  the gift of sight a reality for many more Indians.
The goal is clear: to transform the gift of eye donation into the gift of sight.  Every donated cornea carries a legacy of compassion—allowing one person’s life to bring light into another’s.
(Dr. Mohan Rajan is chairman and medical director and Dr. Sujatha Mohan is executive medical director, of Rajan Eye Care Hospital. drmohanrajan@gmail.com)

title: Out of neglect bin: On perimenopausal policy

content.value: Women’s health care can be accused of being focused entirely on the reproductive age group.
